ADR 0016 specifies an Electron-only mirror that writes derived Markdown under mirror/markdown/journals/ and mirror/markdown/pages/ (ADR 0016) — with the explicit rule that “the DB remains the source of truth” and mirror files feed back into nothing. If you want to understand how a durable local store can back an editor, the SQLite engine behind this design is itself worth a source tour.

Plugins and the Electron Shell

The extension surface is a second ClojureScript namespace reserved for third parties: logseq.api, L2 is documented as “Logseq API for plugins usage” and exports dozens of hooks — slash command registration (register_plugin_slash_command, L53), storage files, user settings, UI items. The host installs during boot via handler.plugin/setup!, L1341. DB-version-specific plugin calls live in logseq.api.db-based, L2 (“DB version related fns”), which routes page and property mutations through the same outliner core the editor uses — plugins get no side door into the database, and block APIs even namespace their properties (plugin.property prefix, L17) to keep plugin data distinguishable from user data. Compared with the compiler-checked, type-first approach we covered in the TypeScript source tour, this is a runtime-gated API: flexible for authors, stricter at the boundary.

On the desktop, the same ClojureScript bundle runs inside Electron. The renderer talks to the main process through electron.ipc/ipc, L28, which serializes payloads as transit strings before calling window.apis.doAction (doAction call, L33) — one typed channel instead of dozens of ad-hoc bridges. The main process owns filesystem primitives (native db.sqlite files, plugin directories, the Markdown mirror), while all content logic stays in the worker per the ADR.

Honest Limits

  • Master is the DB-version branch. The SQLite graph, worker split and mirror ADR describe current master; the classic file-version code paths largely live in release branches and history. Treat master as fast-moving — the README itself steers stability-seekers elsewhere.
  • DB version is beta. The README says data loss is possible and recommends backups; real-time collaboration is in alpha. The sync libraries exist in-tree (db-sync dep, L46) but the surrounding product surface is explicitly unfinished.
  • The Markdown mirror is one-way. Editing mirrored files does not update the graph, per ADR 0016; it is an export, not round-trip sync, and browser/mobile builds do not get it.
  • Datascript is still in memory. Durability comes from the SQLite storage layer, so very large graphs trade RAM for query speed; the kvs-table design (create-kvs-table!, L10) is the boundary where that trade is managed.
  • Docs drift. src/main/frontend/persist_db/README.md still describes the older in-memory mental model, so older tutorials can disagree with newer code about where the database lives.
entry.summary: How Logseq works inside: the ClojureScript outliner frontend, Datascript EDN datoms on SQLite, the DB worker split, Datalog queries and the plugin API.

entry.title: How NocoDB Works: Inside the Airtable Alternative Architecture

link.title: How NocoDB Works: Inside the Airtable Alternative Architecture

entry.content:
Your production data already lives in a Postgres or MySQL instance, carefully backed up, replicated, and monitored. Then a teammate wants “something like Airtable” for it, and the conventional answer is to export tables into a SaaS spreadsheet, run nightly sync scripts, and accept that the two copies drift apart the moment someone edits either side. Row caps, API rate limits, and per-seat pricing pile on top of the real problem: the spreadsheet never touches the database you actually run. NocoDB’s open-source bet is that this copy step is unnecessary — it boots a NestJS server, connects to your existing database as one more client, and serves a Vue spreadsheet UI whose every cell reads and writes that database in place.

This post is a source tour of how that works, verified line by line against the nocodb/nocodb repository on its develop branch. The overview diagram below traces the full request path: the Vue grid in packages/nc-gui, the NestJS controllers and services in packages/nocodb, the Knex-based SQL engine, and the two storage layers — the nc_ metadata tables and your own data. The detail diagram then zooms into each layer, from the server bootstrap down to individual view models.

If you have ever wondered what “Airtable alternative” means structurally — where the smart spreadsheet ends and the database begins, which tables NocoDB creates, and how a filter you click in the UI becomes a WHERE clause — the next two diagrams and five sections answer exactly that, with links into the source at every step.

Overview: a click in the Vue grid travels through the NestJS controller and service layers into BaseModelSqlv2, which builds Knex queries against your database, while all spreadsheet metadata stays in the separate nc_ tables.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The server entry point is Noco.init, L165, which calls NestFactory.create, L166 with AppModule and a disabled body parser — NestJS boots on top of the plain Express instance created in bootstrap, L17, so there is exactly one HTTP server and one process.
  • Every spreadsheet operation arrives as REST: DataTableController, L26 maps GET /api/v2/tables/:modelId/records, L30 and POST records, L75 — the same endpoints the frontend SDK calls.
  • Controllers are thin: DataTableService.dataList, L58 resolves the model and view, then hands off to DatasService, L49, which owns actual row execution.
  • The bridge between metadata and SQL is Model.getBaseModelSQL, L649: it reads the model’s column definitions and constructs new BaseModelSqlv2, L693 with the driver for that source.
  • BaseModelSqlv2, L326 is the row engine — list, insert (insert, L2455), update, delete, link resolution — built as knex query builders, never raw string SQL.
  • Queries flow through a customized Knex: conditionv2, L1625 is a QueryBuilder extension that compiles NocoDB’s nested filter tree objects into WHERE clauses, and the whole module is exported as XKnex, L1698.
  • Database connections are pooled per source by NcConnectionMgrv2, L27, which keeps an LRU of drivers, L35 and builds each one with XKnex(config), L189 on first use.
  • The spreadsheet layer itself lives in MetaService, L41 — a knex instance over config.meta.db (metaDbConfig, L63) that reads and writes the nc_*_v2 tables declared in the MetaTable enum, L1, including nc_bases_v2 (L2), nc_grid_view_v2 (L34), and nc_kanban_view_v2 (L36).

Detail view: the bootstrap chain, the controller→service→model funnel, the SQL engine internals, and the Vue composables — 33 nodes covering every layer cited in this post.

The request path: from a grid cell to a Postgres query

Consider the smallest unit of work: the user types into a cell and the grid saves it. In the frontend, the grid surface wires its data through useViewData, L228, a composable defined in useViewData.ts, L13 whose loadData function issues api.dbViewRow.list, L266 — a typed SDK call against /api/v2/tables/:modelId/records. The virtualized InfiniteTable.vue, L272 keeps calling loadData({ offset, limit }) as you scroll, so pagination is just offset queries against the real table.

On the server, that request lands in the controller, moves through the service, and reaches BaseModelSqlv2, which knows three things: the table’s real name and columns (from metadata), the active view’s filters and sorts (also from metadata), and a knex driver for the source. It composes those into one SQL statement and sends it through the source’s pool. Relation fields — the linked-records columns that make a spreadsheet “smart” — get special treatment: the engine attaches batched loaders guarded by a serial queue (PQueue, L445, default concurrency 1) so resolving hundreds of link cells cannot exhaust the pool.

The HTTP plumbing is worth a pause because it is unusual for a NestJS codebase. NocoDB disables Nest’s body parser and mounts the Nest app as middleware inside an explicitly created Express server — the same one that later serves the built GUI from public/. If you want to see how much behavior hides inside that adapter layer, I traced Express’s internals separately in the Express source walkthrough; here it means one listening socket, no duplicate middleware, and direct access to req.ip for proxy-aware auditing (configured around L225 in Noco.ts).

The meta layer: nc_ tables that never touch your data

NocoDB’s own storage is deliberately small and boring. All of it — workspaces, bases, sources, models, columns, views, hooks, tokens, ACLs — is rows in tables prefixed nc_, named centrally in the MetaTable enum, L1. The v0 migration nc_001_init.ts, L1081 creates nc_bases_v2 with a nc_bases_v2_pkey composite primary key; every later schema change ships as an additional numbered migration file applied by migrate.latest, L1204.

By default this metadata store is a single SQLite file — NcConfig initializes meta.db to SQLite, L16 with filename: 'noco.db' at L18 — which is why a fresh NocoDB deployment works with zero external setup. The SQLite file format is what makes that safe as a config store: single-writer access, plain SQL, trivially backed up. Operators who outgrow it set NC_DB to a Postgres or MySQL URL instead, and MetaService runs identically on top because everything goes through the same knex builder (metaDbConfig, L63).

Every metadata write is workspace/base-scoped by construction: metaInsert2, L350 stamps fk_workspace_id and base_id onto each row and rejects inserts outside valid root scopes, while reads go through metaGet2/metaList2, which append the same scoping WHERE clauses. Record ids are generated per table by genNanoid, L156 using a prefix map (p for bases, m for models, c for columns, vw for views, kv for kanban views) — a small touch that makes every id in the metadata store self-describing in logs and URLs.

Views are metadata, not tables

The most instructive design decision in NocoDB is that grid, kanban, gallery, form, calendar, and timeline views are not data structures of their own — they are metadata projections over the same underlying table. The ViewTypes mapping, L106 in View.ts dispatches each view type to its own nc_*_view_columns_v2 metadata table: grid columns to nc_grid_view_columns_v2, kanban to nc_kanban_view_columns_v2, and so on through nine view types. Creating a view inserts rows there (View.insert, L362), never a new data table.

Each type keeps its specifics in a dedicated model: GridView, L16 stores flags like showSystemFields, KanbanView, L25 stores the stacking column configuration. The frontend consumes this split naturally — the kanban board loads through KanbanOptimized.vue, L547 calling loadKanbanData from a store that groups rows server-side via dbViewRow.groupedDataList, L763, so the stack grouping happens as one GROUP BY query against your database rather than a client-side sort of everything.

This is also why switching between grid and kanban feels instant: the rows are identical, only the projection changes, and filters/sorts are just additional knex clauses injected through the conditionv2 extension before the query executes. When a new column is added, ViewsService syncs column metadata into every existing view so all projections stay consistent — spreadsheet semantics implemented as a handful of small SQL statements.

From Airtable copies to in-place SQL (build facts)

For builders evaluating or extending NocoDB, the load-bearing facts are these. The backend is Node.js with knex 3.1.0 pinned at L142 and dedicated drivers for mysql2, L152, pg, L179, and sqlite3, L197 — the three databases it can attach to as data sources. The web framework pair is @nestjs/core 10.x at L70 with express 4.x at L118, and the whole thing runs in one Node process, so understanding its concurrency model matters before you scale it; my notes on the Node.js event loop cover the ground rules it inherits.

So the transformation NocoDB performs is precise: your table becomes a Model row, your columns become Column rows, your constraints stay in your database untouched, and the smart-spreadsheet experience is recomputed on every request from nc_ metadata plus live queries. Nothing replicates your rows. If you delete a column in NocoDB’s UI, it runs DDL against your database; if you edit a cell, it is an UPDATE on your table — the same consequences as editing via psql, with the spreadsheet as the client.

Two practical consequences follow. First, backup strategy is unchanged — your data backups are still your database backups, plus one extra small artifact (the noco.db meta file or NC_DB instance) that you should snapshot separately, since it holds views, permissions, and hooks. Second, performance is your database’s performance: the grid is as fast as the queries knex emits against your indexes, and no intermediate store will mask a missing index on a column you filter by.

Honest Limits

  • NocoDB reads your schema through its source models but stores its understanding of columns in nc_columns_v2; schema changes made outside NocoDB are not magically reflected — the metadata and the real schema are two stores that the sync/model-diff services reconcile, and drift there is a real operational surface.
  • The serial query queue (concurrency 1 by default) protects pools but also caps parallelism for relation-heavy requests; it is tunable via NC_DB_QUERY_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY per the code at BaseModelSqlv2, L445, and raising it trades throughput against pool exhaustion.
  • Satellite metadata (audit, chat, docs, operation logs) can live on separate databases when environment variables are set, and mixing transactions across them fails loudly by design — the guard is at assertSatelliteNotInMetaTrx, L115.
  • BaseModelSqlv2 dialect handling (for example the per-database random ordering in shuffle, L2421) shows the engine must special-case MySQL, Postgres, SQLite, MSSQL, and Oracle; exotic engines beyond the three shipped drivers are not a drop-in.
  • The metadata id generator uses nanoid variants of fixed length (L33-L38 in meta.service.ts); ids are short by design, so nothing in the nc_ store is intended to be globally unique across independent deployments — merges of two metadata stores are not a supported operation.
entry.summary: How NocoDB turns any MySQL, Postgres, or SQLite database into an Airtable-style smart spreadsheet: NestJS backend, Knex queries, and nc_ meta tables.

entry.title: How Outline Works: Inside the Team Wiki Architecture

link.title: How Outline Works: Inside the Team Wiki Architecture

entry.content:
Ask three people where the API spec lives and you will get three different answers: a Slack thread nobody can find anymore, a Google Doc whose owner left the company, and a Notion page that needs a login half the team does not have. Outline attacks exactly that pain. It is an open-source team wiki that companies self-host, backed by their own PostgreSQL, so every doc, revision and permission lives in one searchable place instead of scattering across SaaS silos. And it is not a weekend toy: the monorepo ships a Node.js and Koa API server, a realtime collaboration server, and a rich editor built from one shared ProseMirror package.

Two diagrams in this post map that promise onto the real source tree. The overview follows a single edit from the React client through a Hocuspocus WebSocket connection into the persistence extension that snapshots the Yjs document back into Postgres, while REST endpoints and Bull queues fan out the consequences. The detail diagram opens the box further: the collaboration extension chain, the four Redis queues with their processors, the SSO auth plugins, and the tsvector indexes that make full-text search a database feature rather than an add-on.

By the end you will know why Outline stores the same document three different ways (ProseMirror JSONB, Yjs state BLOB, search vector), how one keystroke becomes an update, then a revision, then a backlink without ever leaving Postgres, and where the code draws the boundary between the API path and the realtime path. Every symbol cited below carries a line anchor and was verified against the main branch of outline/outline.

Overview: the React client edits through a shared ProseMirror core; realtime edits ride Hocuspocus into Postgres via the persistence extension, REST calls hit the Koa API, and Bull queues on Redis drive the background processors.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The client is React, but the editor is not “a div”. MultiplayerEditor, L87 constructs a CollaborationProvider, L52 — an HocuspocusProvider subclass — per document, bundling socket lifecycle, awareness state and Yjs sync into one object the editor consumes.
  • One editor core shared by client and server. The shared/editor package owns the ProseMirror nodes, marks, plugins and commands; the React app mounts it directly on ProseMirror primitives (EditorView, L27) with an extension manager assembling the stack (ExtensionManager, L39).
  • Realtime is Hocuspocus, tuned and extended. Server.configure, L46 sets debounce to 3000 ms with a 30000 ms timeout, then chains eleven extensions — JWT auth, throttling, connection limits, awareness identity, persistence, API updates, views, logging, metrics.
  • The database is the source of truth, even live. PersistenceExtension, L21 hydrates each Y.Doc straight from the Postgres state column in onLoadDocument, and when state does not exist yet it converts stored ProseMirror content with toYDoc, L90 before persisting it in a transaction.
  • Attribution rides a Redis zset. afterLoadDocument, L119 hooks every document update and records the acting user with zaddWithSequence (zaddWithSequence, L136), so the eventual snapshot knows exactly who edited it.
  • Storing is a snapshot, not a stream. onStoreDocument, L165 encodes the document once with Y.encodeStateAsUpdate (L186) and hands it to documentCollaborativeUpdater (L221), retrying at most maxPersistFailures, L23 — five attempts — before giving up.
  • Background work is Bull on Redis. createQueue, L11 builds Bull queues over shared ioredis clients with stalled/completed/failed metrics; globalEventQueue, L5 is one of four named queues a dedicated worker drains.
  • The REST surface is resource-per-router. apiRouter, L57 composes roughly thirty resource routers — documents, revisions, searches, shares, stars, templates — behind koa-body parsing, CSRF verification and rate limiting.
  • Everything converges on the Document model. Document, L325 holds the content as ProseMirror JSONB (L426) and the Yjs state as a BLOB (L438), publishes domain events after commit, and pings the collaboration server on state changes (notifyCollaborationServer, L664).

Detail: the collaboration service with its extension chain, the Koa API layer over Sequelize models, the Postgres tsvector GIN index, the Bull queue and processor topology, and the SSO auth plugins.

One Codebase, Two Servers

The first thing to internalize is that Outline is two servers in one process tree. The web service is a plain Koa application: init, L25 builds the app and mounts the API, auth, oauth and MCP routers at app.use(mount(routes)), L110. The collaboration service attaches to the same HTTP server’s upgrade event at the /collaboration path (upgrade handler, L76) and hands each WebSocket to Hocuspocus. This Node.js pairing — synchronous REST for reads and writes, asynchronous WebSocket for typing — is the same two-channel pattern we documented in the Node source tour, applied here with a mature CRDT framework instead of hand-rolled messaging.

The extension chain is where Outline customizes Hocuspocus. AuthenticationExtension, L51 resolves the JWT during onAuthenticate (onAuthenticate, L77) and closes connections whose token has expired — the client simply reconnects with a fresh token. Connection limiting, throttling and editor-version checks sit in front, so a misbehaving client is rejected before it can touch a document.

How a Keystroke Becomes a Yjs Update

On the client, ProseMirror and Yjs are bound by the y-prosemirror plugins imported in Multiplayer, L4: the extension gets the shared Y.XmlFragment named default (doc.get, L51) and installs sync, cursor and undo plugins over it. Local edits become Yjs updates; remote updates become ProseMirror transactions. The extension also watches Yjs transactions to attribute each change to a client ID, which is what powers the collaborator badges in the UI.

On the server, the reverse conversion is the interesting part. When the last socket closes, onStoreDocument takes the snapshot and calls documentCollaborativeUpdater, which imports the same ProseMirror schema the editor uses (schema from @server/editor, documentCollaborativeUpdater, L8) and converts the Y.Doc back to ProseMirror JSON with yDocToProsemirrorJSON (L4). That is the trick that keeps one canonical content representation: the Yjs state is the live format, the JSONB column is the projection everyone renders, and ProsemirrorHelper, L150 provides toYDoc and toState, L169 to move between them.

One Postgres, Three Shapes of the Same Document

Outline’s data layer is deliberately boring and therefore worth copying. getDatabaseConfig, L33 hard-codes dialect: "postgres" (L46) — there is no MySQL mode, no pluggable ORM. Sequelize models map every resource, and the three representations of a document live in one documents table: content JSONB for rendering, state BLOB for collaborative continuity, and a searchVector tsvector column maintained by database triggers. The migration documents_team_id_tsv_idx, L10 builds a composite GIN index over (teamId, searchVector) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which is why full-text search stays fast at team scale — this is exactly the Postgres-native search strategy we covered in the Postgres source tour.

The wiki part of “team wiki” is the document tree, and it is a JSONB column too. documentStructure, L276 on the Collection model holds the NavigationNode[] hierarchy, and moving a document rewrites that structure in one place (updateCollectionStructure, L517) instead of shuffling foreign keys across rows. Revisions take a different route: the revisions table (Revision, L36) stores title and content snapshots with collaborator attribution, created asynchronously so typing never waits on history.

Redis Queues Turn Edits Into Revisions, Backlinks and Search

Every meaningful domain change is published as an event after the transaction commits: Event, L88 enqueues the model into globalEventQueue, one of four Bull queues defined in server/queues (global events, processor events, websocket pushes, tasks). The worker service (init, L18) consumes all four and dispatches each event by name to registered processors — the fan-out topology we described in the Redis source tour, but with event routing made explicit in code.

Three processors do most of the wiki housekeeping. RevisionsProcessor, L11 fires on debounced document updates, compares against the latest revision, skips no-op saves, and writes a snapshot through Revision.createFromDocument (L77) — this is why the revision list shows meaningful versions rather than every keystroke. BacklinksProcessor, L17 parses document links and maintains Relationship rows (L133) so “what links here” survives renames and deletes. SearchIndexProcessor, L21 is the interesting negative case: its shouldQueue returns false when the search provider is Postgres (L45), because the tsvector triggers already did the indexing — the queue only carries work for external providers.

From Notion Tabs to a Self-Hosted Wiki: Build Facts Worth Stealing

  • One shared editor package eliminates drift. The shared/editor directory is compiled once and consumed by both the React app and the server-side converters; documentCollaborativeUpdater reuses the identical schema for server rendering, so what users typed is what exports and previews show.
  • Boring storage wins. A single Postgres dialect, one documents table with JSONB plus BLOB plus tsvector, and GIN indexes built CONCURRENTLY — no second database to run until you truly need one.
  • Auth is a plugin folder. Google, Slack, OIDC, Azure, Discord, email and passkeys each live in plugins/<name>/server/auth; the auth router mounts whatever providers exist (auth routes, L97), so adding SSO means adding a folder, not patching a god file.
  • Debounce at the boundary, snapshot at the edge. Hocuspocus debounces 3 seconds and persists once per session end, with a five-attempt retry cap — durable writes without per-keystroke database load.
  • API and realtime write paths converge. REST edits call APIUpdateExtension.notifyUpdate through the Document model hook, and both paths end in documentCollaborativeUpdater, which means one place to enforce validation for every write.
  • Import and export are first-class endpoints. documents.import (documents.import, L1742) and documents.export, L933 make migration from Notion or Markdown a supported operation, processed through dedicated import queues rather than request handlers.

Honest Limits

  • Search beyond Postgres is opt-in and external. The built-in path is tsvector triggers; Elasticsearch-style providers require queue-driven indexing and a running external cluster — the code does not hide this (shouldQueue, L44).
  • Multi-process collaboration fan-out depends on configuration. The Hocuspocus Redis extension is only attached when REDIS_COLLABORATION_URL is set (conditional, L51); a single-instance deployment works without it, but cross-process socket sync needs that Redis.
  • Persistence is capped, not infinite. After five failed snapshot attempts the extension stops retrying that document until new edits arrive (giveUp branch, L237) — resilience by bounded retry, not by queueing writes.
  • Payload size is enforced at the socket. The WebSocket server caps documents at DocumentValidation.maxStateLength (maxPayload, L34) and tolerates oversized-payload errors instead of crashing the process.
  • Identical edits do not create revisions. When the new snapshot equals the previous revision, the processor returns early and clears the attribution zset (skip branch, L50) — revision history records content changes, not comment-only touches.
entry.summary: How Outline's self-hosted team wiki works internally: Koa API, ProseMirror editor, Yjs realtime sync, Postgres storage and search, Redis Bull queues, SSO auth.

entry.title: How SiYuan Works: Inside the Block-Based Note-Taking Kernel Architecture

link.title: How SiYuan Works: Inside the Block-Based Note-Taking Kernel Architecture

entry.content:
Most note apps treat a document as an opaque blob. A paragraph is just a fragment of one big markdown file, so “link to exactly this paragraph” degenerates into text search, “what references this heading” requires re-parsing your whole vault, and transcluding a block means copying text that silently drifts out of date. SiYuan makes the opposite bet: every paragraph, heading, list item, and table row is a first-class block with a stable ID, and the app indexes each one so you can reference, transclude, and query any paragraph the way you would query a database row.

That promise has to be delivered by architecture, not slogans. The two diagrams in this post map how it actually is delivered. The overview shows the shape of the system: an Electron shell and TypeScript editor talking to a Go kernel over HTTP and a WebSocket, with a SQLite index underneath and a snapshot-based sync layer on top. The detail diagram zooms into the write path — from a keystroke in the editor to a transaction, to a re-indexed document tree, to rows landing in the blocks, spans, and refs tables.

Reading the source with that map in hand teaches three concrete things: how a markdown-flavored document gets projected into addressable rows, why backlink queries stay fast without re-parsing files, and how SiYuan syncs content-addressed snapshots instead of shuffling raw files around. Every symbol and line number below is verified against the master branch of the siyuan-note/siyuan repository.

Overview of SiYuan: the TypeScript frontend and the Go kernel meet at one HTTP/WebSocket boundary; all writes funnel through the transaction engine into the SQLite index.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One process boots everything. The kernel’s main, L15 only runs a cobra command; the serve subcommand calls server.Serve, L61 in a goroutine and InitDatabase, L62 on the main one. Electron then just points a BrowserWindow at 127.0.0.1.
  • The server is gin with strict middleware. Serve, L130 builds a gin engine that serializes requests (ControlConcurrency, L144), then registers assets, WebDAV, MCP, and the API (ServeAPI, L184).
  • The editor is a browser view, not a native shell. The Protyle, L127 class opens a WebSocket per document via new WebSocket, L81 against the kernel’s /ws endpoint (serveWebSocket, L1885).
  • Writes arrive as ordered transactions. The editor batches DOM edits and posts them to /api/transactions (fetchPost, L752), where PerformTransactions, L210 replays them server-side — the client never writes SQLite directly.
  • Documents persist as JSON trees. Full indexing loads every .sy file (the suffix check, L278), parses it with the Lute engine, and queues rows via IndexTreeQueue, L641.
  • Every block is a table row. The schema at CREATE TABLE blocks, L179 stores id, parent_id, root_id, hash, box, path, content, markdown, and type per block — the Block struct, L26 mirrors it.
  • Row identity is content-hashed. Each block gets a 7-hex digest computed from its markdown, IAL attributes, and parent (sha256 slice, L55), so identical content produces identical hashes.
  • Search is FTS5 external content. blocks_fts, L332 is a virtual table whose rowids are shared with blocks, giving full-text search without duplicating storage ownership.
  • Backlinks come from a refs table. The refs schema, L284 stores def-block/ref-block pairs; GetBacklink2, L614 turns those rows into the backlink panel in one indexed query.

The detail view: boot chain and transport on top, the model layer in the middle, the SQLite writers at the bottom left, sync and the bazaar on the right.

Why a Go kernel sits behind an Electron window

SiYuan’s packaging is unusual: it ships an Electron desktop app, but the app is mostly a thin shell. The TypeScript side (over two thousand .ts files, zero .vue files — this is plain TypeScript with webpack, package.json, L2) renders tabs, panels, and the Protyle editor, while all state lives in the Go process. That split is what makes block-level features coherent: whether you edit from the desktop app, the browser when serving over the network, or a mobile client, the same kernel serializes writes and broadcasts changes.

The WebSocket is not a nice-to-have; it is the state channel. When the server’s handleWebSocketMessage, L2002 receives a message, it dispatches to session-scoped handlers that push events like document reloads, sync status, and bazaar changes back to every listening tab. The overview’s long edge from the SQLite store back to the editor is exactly this: the editor re-renders from server-pushed state instead of maintaining its own truth. If you want to compare this client-server split with other runtimes, the Go and Node source tours on this blog cover the two most common alternatives.

The write path: keystroke to indexed row

Follow one edit through the detail diagram. The editor computes a diff of your change and serializes it as an operation — insert, update, move, delete of a specific block ID — then POSTs the batch. The route lives in the API router (registerTransactionsRoutes, L716), and the model layer replays the operations in order (PerformTransactions, L210) against the in-memory tree before enqueueing the affected document for re-index.

Re-indexing is differential, not full-scan. The queued tree lands in upsertTreeWithChanges, L441, which writes only the rows that actually changed, and each AST node is projected into its row by buildBlockFromNode, L1000 — filling content, markdown, parent and root IDs in one pass. Inline elements go through buildSpanFromNode, L800: every tag, image, and block-ref TextMark becomes a row in spans (Span struct, L33), which is how SiYuan can list “all blocks with tags” or “all images” without scanning text.

The same pass maintains the link graph. Block references become pairs in refs via upsertRefs, L28, keyed by the definition block they point at. That is the trick behind backlinks and mentions: RefreshBacklink, L28 recomputes per-document, and queries like GetBacklinkDoc, L262 join the refs table against the blocks table — indexed lookups instead of full-text scans. This is the same insight that relational SQLite designs exploit everywhere: precompute relationships at write time so reads stay cheap.

Blocks, trees, and seven-hex-char hashes

Storage has three layers that many people conflate. On disk, a document is one .sy file — a JSON serialization of the block tree — named after its root block ID; the rename logic that keeps file name and root ID in lockstep appends the ID to the path (the .sy path join, L68). In memory, the tree is a Lute AST (SiYuan’s markdown engine, imported at tree.go, L17). In the index, the same tree is rows in blocks with parent/child and root columns rebuilt from the AST hierarchy.

The hash column deserves attention because it encodes identity, not just checksums. NodeHashWithHeadingParent, L31 digests the notebook and path, the sorted IAL attributes, the formatted markdown, and the parent ID, then keeps the first 7 hex characters of the sha256. Change any of those inputs and the hash changes, which lets the index detect real edits cheaply and lets history views tell “you retyped it” from “nothing changed”. The full-text index rides along: blocks_fts is declared with content='blocks' (FTS5 virtual table, L332), so the tokenizer reads straight from the blocks table by rowid rather than owning a second copy of the text — and the schema comment notes the tokenizer is fixed at creation time, so changing tokenization requires an explicit rebuild.

From Markdown blobs to SQLite rows: build facts

A few verified facts for anyone building on top of this stack. The kernel is a single Go module: SQLite through mattn/go-sqlite3 with a registered sqlite3_extended driver (sql.Register, L67), routing through gin, WebSockets through melody (melody.New, L1886), markdown through 88250/lute, and sync through siyuan-note/dejavu (imported at repository.go, L37). The frontend is Electron 44 with TypeScript and webpack (electron, L85), building desktop, mobile, and export bundles from the same sources. Historically this codebase migrated from a Python-free pure-frontend design into today’s split: documents that used to be loose markdown files became .sy JSON trees, and text indexes that used to be ad-hoc became the FTS5-backed blocks projection — the direction of travel is always “make the block addressable”. The API surface is stable enough that plugins, and the bazaar listing at GetUpdatedPackages, L211, can extend the kernel without forking it.

Sync: snapshot deltas over four providers

Sync is built on snapshots, not file copies. The kernel wraps the dejavu engine (repository.go exposes snapshot listing, diffing, and rollback at GetRepoSnapshots, L1061), and SyncData, L272 drives boot-time, scheduled, and manual syncs through one path. The provider switch is explicit in config: official cloud (ProviderSiYuan), S3-compatible object storage, WebDAV, and a local filesystem provider (provider constants, L71); SetSyncProvider, L699 validates the endpoint before committing. Because the units of transfer are content-addressed snapshot files, the same mechanism serves version history and rollback — restoring a document is a checkout, not a “recently edited files” heuristic. Conflicts are detected rather than last-write-wins, and the WebSocket pushes sync state so open tabs react when another device changes the workspace.

Honest Limits

  • The SQLite index is a projection, not the source of truth. The .sy files remain canonical; the kernel even skips indexing encrypted notebooks entirely (the encrypted-box guard, L143), so encrypted content is searchable only after decryption.
  • The block hash is truncated to 7 hex characters (L55). It is a change-detection key, not a cryptographic guarantee against collisions.
  • The FTS5 tokenizer is fixed when blocks_fts is created (L332); switching case sensitivity or tokenization requires a rebuild, it is not a live setting.
  • refs rows are built during indexing (upsertRefs, L28), so external tools editing .sy files on disk will not appear in backlinks until the kernel re-indexes them.
  • Request serialization is deliberate: the kernel processes API requests one at a time (ControlConcurrency, L144), trading throughput for consistency on a single-user desktop workload.
entry.summary: Inside SiYuan's Go kernel: how notes become SQLite block rows, how transactions, backlinks and FTS5 search work, and how snapshot sync keeps notebooks current.
